one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes an Easter Sunday wellness/lifestyle/longevity reflection -- Easter commemorates the resurrection of Christ and the fulfillment of His promise to rise on the third day, celebrating His gift of eternal and earthly life; for now, however, CJP writes of earthly life. The youngest in a brood of four who are all still alive, he reached his 78th birthday last December; his eldest sibling, now 87, lives in retirement with her husband in Vancouver. He and his siblings are luckier than their parents -- his father died at 54 and his mother at 61 -- and the entire generation can expect to live 20 years longer than the previous one (by which measure CJP would be only 58); per Time magazine (March 2, 2015), American babies born today could live 142 years thanks to science, technology, medicine, and improved lifestyles. He has had brushes with ill health: at 5 during the Japanese occupation he nearly died of dysentery; at 21 while chairing a National Union of Students of the Philippines seminar in Naga City, his ruptured appendix was misdiagnosed as ordinary stomachache in a small clinic in Tabaco, Albay -- given castor oil (!) and injected with morphine which knocked him out for 24 hours -- and two weeks later, the ruptured appendix ached again, was properly diagnosed, and excised surgically by Dr. Ricardo Alfonso. In 1983, Dr. Augusto Litonjua told him 'I am sorry to say you have diabetes. This is incurable but can be controlled by diet, exercise and a little medicine.' He followed the prescription to the letter -- and voila! -- in 1995, prior to his SC entry, Dr. Litonjua formally certified his blood sugar had normalized; his diabetes was gone. He continues to see Litonjua every three months for regular consultation especially on endocrinal secretions. In 1996, Dr. Dante Morales, after three tests (ECG, treadmill, 2D Echo) said he had arrhythmia and may need heart bypass surgery; before the OR, Morales asked Dr. Dy Bun Yok to do an angiogram, with Dr. Jorge Garcia (famous heart surgeon) ready to operate if the angiogram affirmed the three earlier tests. To his complete relief, the final test showed no blocked coronary arteries -- no surgery needed; Dr. Garcia kidded afterwards: 'When you die, it will not be because of a heart problem.' Alleluia! In 2008, while playing golf with Dr. Jack Arroyo, even in bright sunlight he could not see his driven ball 200 yards away on the turf; at the American Eye Center he was advised to undergo cataract surgery. 'I do cataracts, but Dr. Cesar Espiritu is the best cataract surgeon,' Dr. Arroyo humbly said; at his recommendation, Dr. Espiritu replaced his clouded crystalline lenses with artificial implants. Since then his vision has been 20/20 -- if he still sports eyeglasses, it is because his dear wife believes it more becoming for a retired chief justice. He has undergone other medical procedures and conditions: three surgeries for recurrent hemorrhoids in 1958, 1977, and 2005; a biopsy of his prostate by Dr. Nikko Magsanoc which turned out negative; a whole-body MRI in 2012 which showed gallstones and benign liver and kidney cysts; various dental problems; slowed memory retrieval; insomnia; bladder spasms; vertigo; elevated SGPT/SGOT; bone spurs; pulled muscles; stem cell therapy; carpal tunnel syndrome. He is grateful for these medical interventions. Thank God, even in his senior years he can eat almost anything in moderate quantities -- plays golf twice a week and tennis twice a week, exercises in the gym thrice a week, indulges occasionally in ballroom dancing, does not smoke, gamble, or drink anything heavier than a glass of red wine. Retired from the judiciary eight years ago but not from work, his every day is full: board and committee meetings of a dozen publicly listed companies, heading or advising five major foundations and several educational/civic/religious/charitable groups. He enjoys writing this column (encoding it on his own computer to polish typing and keep up with current events), reads printed and digital Inquirer and other publications/books, surfs the Internet, tracks stock markets, watches TV news, science programs (Discovery Science, History Channel), and sports. He maintains a personal website but no social-media account; he likes his new iPhone 6 plus over the iPad and old Nokia. He has an active social life -- diplomatic receptions, concerts, art exhibits, birthdays, weddings, charities -- and prays for the eternal joy and peace of the deceased during wakes. He thanks God for giving him more years than his parents, is grateful to his family and friends who forgive his lapses, laugh at his jokes, and make him feel younger than his age, and is especially thankful to his doctors and priest-counselors. He looks forward to 'more years in my life and more life in my years.'
